summary:
John stands apart from the other three gospels — most of what it records appears in none of them — and it announces its purpose outright: that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that by believing you may have life in his name. Unlike the other gospels, John opens not with a birth narrative but with a cosmic declaration that echoes the first words of Genesis: Jesus is the eternal Word (Logos) who was with God and was God, and who became flesh and lived among humanity. Everything in the gospel flows from this claim. The book's closing lines credit the account to an unnamed eyewitness, "the disciple whom Jesus loved," whom church tradition has identified as the apostle John.

John builds his account around miraculous signs — acts that point beyond themselves to who Jesus is — and readers usually count seven. In order, they are: water turned to wine at a wedding in Cana, the healing of an official's dying son, the healing of a man who had been an invalid for thirty-eight years, the feeding of five thousand, a walk across the sea, the giving of sight to a man born blind, and the raising of Lazarus after four days in the tomb. There are no parables in this gospel and no exorcisms. And where the other gospels keep Jesus mostly in Galilee until the final week, much of John takes place in Jerusalem at the festivals — John mentions three Passovers, the main reason Jesus' ministry is usually reckoned at about three years. The signs divide the crowds: some believe, some report him to the Pharisees, and the raising of Lazarus becomes the breaking point — "So from that day on they plotted to kill Him."

In place of parables, John gives conversations, and they follow a pattern: Jesus says something, the listener takes him literally, and the misunderstanding opens the way to what he really means. Nicodemus, a Pharisee who comes by night, hears "You must be born again" and asks how an old man can re-enter the womb. A Samaritan woman, offered "living water," points out that Jesus has nothing to draw with — yet she becomes the first person to whom he openly says he is the Messiah. A crowd fed on loaves comes back for more bread and is told, "I am the bread of life." And it is in the conversation with Nicodemus that John 3:16 appears: "For God so loved the world that He gave His one and only Son, that everyone who believes in Him shall not perish but have eternal life."

Jesus completes "I am" with seven pictures: the bread of life, the light of the world, the gate, the good shepherd, the resurrection and the life, the way and the truth and the life, the true vine. Sometimes he uses the bare phrase alone — "before Abraham was born, I am!" — an echo of the name God revealed to Moses at the burning bush (Exodus 3:14), and his hearers pick up stones. When he adds, "I and the Father are one," the stones come out again, and this time the charge is spelled out: "You, who are a man, make Yourself out to be God."

At Cana Jesus tells his mother, "My hour has not yet come," and that refrain holds until the final Passover, when the hour arrives. On his last night he washes his disciples' feet, commands them to love one another as he has loved them, promises the Holy Spirit as "another Advocate," and prays for everyone who will believe through their message. Even the arrest bears his stamp: when he says "I am He," the soldiers draw back and fall to the ground. He carries his own cross, tells Pilate he has come to testify to the truth — "What is truth?" the governor replies — and dies declaring, "It is finished" — one word in John's Greek, tetelestai.

The resurrection unfolds in quiet recognitions. Mary Magdalene mistakes Jesus for the gardener until he says her name. Thomas swears he will not believe without touching the wounds; eight days later, invited to do exactly that, he answers with the words the whole book has been building toward: "My Lord and my God!" The gospel that opened by calling the Word God ends with a man saying it to Jesus' face — and Jesus' reply reaches past Thomas to the reader: "blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed." A final chapter adds breakfast on the shore and Peter restored with three questions matching his three denials, and the book signs off by admitting its own limits: if everything Jesus did were written down, "not even the world itself would have space for the books that would be written."
